# Elastic Load Balancing: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q010 -->
### Question 1

A company hosts three websites, example.com, example.net and example.org, on Amazon EC2 instances behind one Application Load Balancer. Host-based listener rules send the requests of each website to its own target group. The company must now encrypt the traffic in transit between users and the load balancer, and every website must stay on port 443. Each website has its own public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create HTTPS listeners on ports 443, 8443 and 9443, one per website, and attach that website's ACM certificate to each.
- Create three Application Load Balancers, one per website, each with an HTTPS listener on port 443 and that website's ACM certificate.
- Replace the load balancer with a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and install each website's certificate on the instances.
- Create one HTTPS listener on port 443, and add all three ACM certificates to the certificate list of that listener.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one HTTPS listener on port 443, and add all three ACM certificates to the certificate list of that listener.

**Deciding phrases.** "example.com, example.net and example.org", "every website must stay on port 443", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: three websites with different parent domains, host rules on one load balancer, encryption in transit to the load balancer, port 443 for every website, and one ACM certificate for each website.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict one HTTPS listener on port 443 with all three certificates, because a certificate list lets one listener serve several domains on the same port, and SNI picks the certificate.
4. I remove the listeners on ports 8443 and 9443, because every website must stay on port 443. I remove the Network Load Balancer, because it works at layer 4 and would lose the host rules.
5. Between the certificate list and three load balancers, the difference is how much the team must run and change; the stem says LEAST operational overhead, so one listener with one set of rules wins over three load balancers with three listeners.
6. Check: the certificate list keeps port 443, keeps the host rules and uses the three ACM certificates. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The three names have different parent domains, so one wildcard certificate does not cover them. One HTTPS listener holds a default certificate plus a certificate list, and [SNI is automatically enabled](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates) when the listener has [more than one TLS certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-faq-sni-automatic-multiple-certificates). The load balancer reads the host name that the client sends and presents the matching certificate.

**Why not.**

- "Create HTTPS listeners on ports 443, 8443 and ...": Every website must stay on port 443, and one listener can serve them all, because a certificate list can [provide a different certificate for each domain](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains).
- "Create three Application Load Balancers, one per website, ...": Three load balancers mean three listeners and three sets of rules to run and change, where one listener with a certificate list is enough.
- "Replace the load balancer with a Network Load ...": A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type), so the host-based rules are lost, and every instance then needs its own certificates.

**Twin.** If the stem said "shop.example.com, help.example.com and news.example.com" instead: one certificate could cover all three, because you can [use a wildcard certificate](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cert-wildcard-or-san-single-cert).

**Takeaway.** Several HTTPS domains on one port: one listener with a certificate list, and SNI picks the certificate.

**Review.** [An HTTPS listener decrypts requests at the load balancer with its certificate](2-deep.md#an-https-listener-decrypts-requests-at-the-load-balancer-with-its-certificate-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an API on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one VPC. Listener rules send /orders/* and /reports/* to separate target groups. A large customer now requires a fixed set of IP addresses that it can allow-list in its firewall. The path-based routing must stay in place, and the company uses one AWS Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer that has an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and move the path rules to its listener.
- Associate an Elastic IP address with the Application Load Balancer node in each subnet, and give the customer those addresses to allow-list.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register the existing Application Load Balancer as its target.
- Launch Amazon EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses that run reverse proxy software, and have them forward every request to the Application Load Balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register the existing Application Load Balancer as its target.

**Deciding phrases.** "requires a fixed set of IP addresses", "The path-based routing must stay in place", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: the customer needs a fixed set of IP addresses, the /orders/* and /reports/* path rules must stay, and everything runs in one VPC in one Region.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a swap: replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, because the Network Load Balancer is the type with static and Elastic IP addresses.
4. I remove the Elastic IP addresses on the Application Load Balancer nodes, because the feature table gives static and Elastic IP addresses to the Network Load Balancer only. I remove the proxy instances, because the company would have to run and patch them.
5. Between the swap and a Network Load Balancer in front of the Application Load Balancer, the difference is the path rules. My first idea breaks because a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and picks a target with a flow hash, so the path rules would be lost. The stem says the rules must stay, so I keep the Application Load Balancer as the target of the Network Load Balancer.
6. Check: the Elastic IP addresses stay fixed, the Application Load Balancer keeps its rules, and both load balancers sit in the same VPC of one account. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The customer needs fixed addresses, and the API still needs rules that read the URL. A Network Load Balancer gives [static IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-static-ip-privatelink) and forwards to an ALB-type target group, where the ALB keeps its path rules. Both load balancers must be [in the same VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-alb-target-same-vpc-same-account), which the stem gives.

**Why not.**

- "Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network ...": A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it has no /orders/* or /reports/* path rules.
- "Associate an Elastic IP address with the Application ...": The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.
- "Launch Amazon EC2 instances with Elastic IP addresses ...": It works, but the company has to patch, scale and replace the proxy instances itself, where a managed Network Load Balancer does the same job.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company uses two AWS Regions" instead: AWS Global Accelerator, because it gives [static IP addresses that serve as fixed endpoints](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-global-accelerator-static-ips) for [load balancers in one or more AWS Regions](../facts/elb.md#elb-ga-alb-multiple-regions).

**Takeaway.** Fixed IP addresses plus path rules: put a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses in front of the ALB.

**Review.** [A Network Load Balancer gives static IP addresses and can keep client IPs](2-deep.md#a-network-load-balancer-gives-static-ip-addresses-and-can-keep-client-ips-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. A team builds a new feature that answers requests for the path /convert. The team wants a serverless solution, so that no instances need to be managed for this feature. The requests and the responses are small JSON documents. The rest of the application must stay unchanged. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Network Load Balancer with a target group of type lambda, register the AWS Lambda function, and send the requests for the path to it.
- Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that receives the requests for the path from the load balancer and invokes the AWS Lambda function for each request.
- Create a target group of type lambda, register the AWS Lambda function in it, and add a listener rule that forwards the path to the target group.
- Create a Gateway Load Balancer in front of the AWS Lambda function, and route the requests for the path through a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a target group of type lambda, register the AWS Lambda function in it, and add a listener rule that forwards the path to the target group.

**Deciding phrases.** "serverless solution", "no instances need to be managed", "requests for the path /convert", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Application Load Balancers are [the only load balancers that support](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-alb-only) the lambda target type. [The target is a Lambda function](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-target-types-instance-ip-lambda) when the target group has the type lambda, and a listener rule for /convert forwards the requests to it. The function runs with no instances, and the other listener rules stay unchanged.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Network Load Balancer with a target ...": Network Load Balancers cannot hold this target group, because Application Load Balancers are [the only load balancers that support](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-alb-only) the lambda target type.
- "Launch an Amazon EC2 instance that receives the ...": It works, but the proxy is one more instance to patch, scale and pay for, which the serverless requirement wanted to avoid.
- "Create a Gateway Load Balancer in front of ...": A Gateway Load Balancer is for [deploying inline virtual appliances](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) such as firewalls, not for running application code behind a path.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each request uploads a video of several hundred megabytes" instead: keep the path on instances or containers, because a Lambda target takes a request body of at most [1 MB](../facts/elb.md#elb-lambda-target-body-max-1-mb).

**Takeaway.** A path of an Application Load Balancer can run a Lambda function through a target group of type lambda.

**Review.** [Each load balancer type reads a different layer of the traffic](2-deep.md#each-load-balancer-type-reads-a-different-layer-of-the-traffic-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Sometimes the application process on an instance hangs. The EC2 status checks of that instance still pass, and the load balancer marks the target as unhealthy. The instance stays in service for days until an engineer terminates it by hand. The company wants to automate the replacement of these instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Lower the unhealthy threshold of the target group health check, so that the load balancer terminates and replaces the hung instances sooner.
- Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs an AWS Lambda function every minute to terminate the instances that the load balancer reports as unhealthy.
- Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, so that in-flight requests finish before the load balancer removes the hung instances.
- Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that instances that fail the load balancer health check are replaced.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group, so that instances that fail the load balancer health check are replaced.

**Deciding phrases.** "EC2 status checks of that instance still pass", "the load balancer marks the target as unhealthy", "automate the replacement", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** By default, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling [ignores the results of the Elastic Load Balancing](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-health-checks-ignored-by-default) health checks, so a hung instance with passing EC2 status checks stays in service. For the ELB health check type, [you must turn it on](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-health-elb-check-must-be-turned-on) for the group. After that, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace), and [Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling replaces the unhealthy instance](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace).

**Why not.**

- "Lower the unhealthy threshold of the target group ...": On a failed check, [Elastic Load Balancing stops sending traffic to it](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-elb-checks-reroute-and-replace); the load balancer itself terminates and launches nothing.
- "Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that runs an ...": It works, but the team writes and maintains code for a check that the Auto Scaling group performs after one setting change.
- "Increase the deregistration delay of the target group, ...": The delay waits so that in-flight requests can finish when a target leaves; it detects no hung process and launches no instance.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instances are not in an Auto Scaling group" instead: nothing replaces them, because on a failed check [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume) and launches nothing.

**Takeaway.** The load balancer routes around an unhealthy target; an Auto Scaling group with ELB health checks replaces it.

**Review.** [Health checks decide which registered targets receive requests](2-deep.md#health-checks-decide-which-registered-targets-receive-requests-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs six small web applications in one AWS Region. Each application has its own domain name, its own Amazon EC2 instances and its own Application Load Balancer. Each load balancer has an HTTPS listener on port 443 with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate for its domain. Traffic to every application is low, but the load balancers run all day. Users must keep reaching each application at its current URL. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, and lower the idle timeout of each load balancer so that unused connections close sooner.
- Replace the six load balancers with one Network Load Balancer that has six TLS listeners, one listener on a different port for each application.
- Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, and turn off cross-zone load balancing on each target group to avoid data transfer charges.
- Use one Application Load Balancer with one HTTPS listener that holds all six certificates, and add host-header rules that forward to six target groups.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use one Application Load Balancer with one HTTPS listener that holds all six certificates, and add host-header rules that forward to six target groups.

**Deciding phrases.** "six small web applications", "its own Application Load Balancer", "keep reaching each application at its current URL", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Each load balancer is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs, so six load balancers bring six hourly charges. One Application Load Balancer can [route requests to multiple domains](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-host-conditions-many-domains-one-lb) with host conditions. Its HTTPS listener can [provide a different certificate for each domain](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sni-certificate-list-multiple-domains) through a certificate list. Users keep their URLs, and five of the six hourly charges go away.

**Why not.**

- "Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, ...": Each load balancer is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs, so six hourly charges stay; the idle timeout changes none of them.
- "Replace the six load balancers with one Network ...": A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and does not read host names, so each application needs its own port, and the URLs change.
- "Keep one Application Load Balancer for each application, ...": With an Application Load Balancer, [you are not charged](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cross-zone-no-data-transfer-charge) for regional data transfer of cross-zone traffic, so this saves nothing.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the applications accept raw TCP connections on their own ports" instead: one Network Load Balancer with a listener per port, because it works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type).

**Takeaway.** Several HTTPS domains can share one Application Load Balancer through host rules and a certificate list.

**Review.** [Listener rules are checked in priority order and the default rule comes last](2-deep.md#listener-rules-are-checked-in-priority-order-and-the-default-rule-comes-last-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A solutions architect reviews the design of a new internet-facing TCP application on Amazon EC2 instances. In the design, a Network Load Balancer has one subnet, in Availability Zone A, and all the instances run in Availability Zone A. The application must be highly available and must keep serving clients if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Replace the instances in Availability Zone A with larger instance types so that the remaining instances can carry the load when one instance fails.
- Give the Network Load Balancer a subnet in Availability Zone B as well, so that it has a load balancer node in each of the two zones.
- Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group so that the load balancer node in Availability Zone A can also use targets in other zones.
- Run instances in Availability Zone B as well, for example with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones and registers its instances with the target group.
- Create a second Network Load Balancer with a subnet in Availability Zone B, and use Amazon Route 53 failover records to switch clients between the two load balancers.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Give the Network Load Balancer a subnet in Availability Zone B as well, so that it has a load balancer node in each of the two zones.
- Run instances in Availability Zone B as well, for example with an Auto Scaling group that spans both zones and registers its instances with the target group.

**Deciding phrases.** "one subnet, in Availability Zone A", "all the instances run in Availability Zone A", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** If Availability Zone A fails, everything in it stops, so the load balancer and the targets both need a second zone. When a zone has no healthy target, the Network Load Balancer removes the address of the [corresponding subnet from DNS](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-unhealthy-az-removed-from-dns-fail-open), and clients reach the node in the healthy zone.

- When you enable a zone, Elastic Load Balancing [creates a load balancer node](../facts/elb.md#elb-node-per-enabled-az) there, so clients keep an entry point if Availability Zone A fails.
- AWS asks you to [avoid single points of failure, including the underlying physical infrastructure](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-rel10-bp01-avoid-single-points-of-failure); instances in a second zone do that for the targets.

**Why not.**

- "Replace the instances in Availability Zone A with ...": Larger instances still run in one zone, so the loss of Availability Zone A still stops the whole application.
- "Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target ...": Cross-zone load balancing uses the [registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does), and here one zone is enabled and holds every instance.
- "Create a second Network Load Balancer with a ...": It works with instances in both zones, but it adds a second load balancer and DNS failover records, where one load balancer with two zones does the same.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instances already run in both zones" instead: enable the second zone alone, because until then [these registered targets do not receive traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-in-disabled-az-no-traffic).

**Takeaway.** To survive a zone failure, the load balancer needs a node and healthy targets in a second zone.

**Review.** [A load balancer gives each enabled Availability Zone its own node](2-deep.md#a-load-balancer-gives-each-enabled-availability-zone-its-own-node-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

- Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
- Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.

**Deciding phrases.** "Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances", "MOST cost-effectively"

**Why.** The load balancer has to read the URL of each request. An Application Load Balancer [functions at the application layer](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-layer-7), and a listener rule with a [path-pattern](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-condition-types) condition sends /api/* requests to a second target group. One load balancer does the whole job, so it is also the cheapest design.

**Why not.**

- "Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic ...": A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and picks a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection), so it cannot send /api/* requests to a separate group.
- "Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic ...": It works, but the company pays for two load balancers, and each one is billed for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour) that it runs.
- "Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic ...": The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the addresses must never change" instead: a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses, because you can [optionally associate one Elastic IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip) for each zone [when you create the Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip).

**Takeaway.** Routing by URL path needs Application Load Balancer listener rules, and one ALB can serve several target groups.

**Review.** [Each load balancer type reads a different layer of the traffic](2-deep.md#each-load-balancer-type-reads-a-different-layer-of-the-traffic-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company is moving an HTTP web application to Amazon EC2 instances that run across multiple Availability Zones in one AWS Region. Business partners call the application from their own networks over the internet. The company needs one entry point in front of the instances that keeps serving requests when an instance fails. Each partner must allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses, and the addresses must never change. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

- Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener rule that forwards /api/* requests to a second target group and all other requests to the first target group.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.
- Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet, and register as its target an Application Load Balancer that has a /api/* listener rule.
- Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic IP address with its node in each subnet, and forward all requests to one target group of the instances.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic IP address in each subnet and a TCP listener that forwards all requests to one target group of the instances.

**Deciding phrases.** "allow-list the load balancer's IP addresses", "the addresses must never change", "MOST cost-effectively"

**Why.** The partners need fixed addresses. In the AWS feature table, [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) belongs to the Network Load Balancer. In each zone, Elastic Load Balancing creates a network interface and [uses it to get a static IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip), while an ALB's node [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap). No HTTP routing is needed, so one load balancer is enough.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Application Load Balancer with a listener ...": Elastic Load Balancing [scales your load balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) and keeps a [time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap) on its DNS entry, so the [IP addresses can be remapped quickly](../facts/elb.md#elb-dns-ttl-60-seconds-remap).
- "Create a Network Load Balancer with one Elastic ...": It gives fixed addresses too, but the extra Application Load Balancer adds a second charge for [each hour or partial hour](../facts/elb.md#elb-partial-hour-billed-as-full-hour).
- "Create an Application Load Balancer, associate one Elastic ...": The feature table lists [IP address - Static, Elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-static-elastic-ip-nlb-only) for the Network Load Balancer only, so an Application Load Balancer node takes no Elastic IP address.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Requests for /api/* must go to a separate group of instances" instead: an Application Load Balancer with a path rule, because it can [forward requests based on the URL](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-path-conditions-smaller-services).

**Takeaway.** Fixed IP addresses for a partner allow-list point to a Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses.

**Review.** [A Network Load Balancer gives static IP addresses and can keep client IPs](2-deep.md#a-network-load-balancer-gives-static-ip-addresses-and-can-keep-client-ips-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. Clients connect over HTTPS on port 443 through a new load balancer. The company wants to protect the data in transit on every network hop. The load balancer must route each request to a target group by its URL path. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

- Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTP target group of the instances on port 80.
- Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTPS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
- Use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, and forward the connections to a TCP target group of the instances, which hold certificates.
- Use a Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the connections to a TLS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener that has an ACM certificate, and forward the requests to an HTTPS target group of the instances, which hold certificates.

**Deciding phrases.** "protect the data in transit on every network hop", "route each request to a target group by its URL path", "MOST secure"

**Why.** The path rule needs a [Layer 7](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) load balancer, so the choice is an Application Load Balancer. Its HTTPS listener uses its certificate to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts) and read the request. An HTTPS target group then opens a second TLS connection to each instance, so both hops are encrypted. [The load balancer does not validate these certificates](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-target-https-no-cert-validation), so self-signed ones work.

**Why not.**

- "Use an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS ...": The HTTPS listener uses its certificate to [terminate the front-end connection](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-listener-terminates-and-decrypts), so the hop to the instances carries plain HTTP.
- "Use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP ...": A Network Load Balancer works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and passes the encrypted bytes through, so it cannot read the URL path to choose a target group.
- "Use a Network Load Balancer with a TLS ...": A TLS listener decrypts, but a Network Load Balancer still works at [Layer 4](../facts/elb.md#elb-compare-layer-per-type) and does not read the URL path.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Each instance must decrypt the client traffic with its own certificate and private key" instead: the Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443, because it [passes encrypted traffic through to the targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-https-decrypt-at-target-use-nlb-tcp).

**Takeaway.** Path routing needs an Application Load Balancer; an HTTPS target group encrypts the hop to the instances.

**Review.** [Encryption to the targets needs a second TLS connection or a pass-through](2-deep.md#encryption-to-the-targets-needs-a-second-tls-connection-or-a-pass-through-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q015 -->
### Question 10

A company serves a website through an Application Load Balancer that has an HTTPS listener on port 443 with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate. The load balancer has no other listener. Users who enter the website address with HTTP in the browser receive an error. The company wants these users to reach the HTTPS site, so that all requests are encrypted in transit. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add an HTTP listener on port 80 that forwards requests to the instances, and change the application code to return a redirect to HTTPS.
- Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action returns a fixed response that asks users to enter the HTTPS address in the browser.
- Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action redirects every request to HTTPS on port 443 with a permanent HTTP 301 response.
- Create a second Application Load Balancer with an HTTP listener on port 80, and point a second DNS name for the website at that load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose default action redirects every request to HTTPS on port 443 with a permanent HTTP 301 response.

**Deciding phrases.** "The load balancer has no other listener", "receive an error", "reach the HTTPS site", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** One Application Load Balancer can have listeners on [HTTP port 80](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb) and [HTTPS port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb). A redirect action on the new port 80 listener sends [HTTP to HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https), so the browser repeats the request over TLS. The load balancer does the work, and the application code stays unchanged.

**Why not.**

- "Add an HTTP listener on port 80 that ...": It works, but the team writes, tests and deploys code for a redirect that the load balancer can return by itself.
- "Add an HTTP listener on port 80 whose ...": A fixed-response action [returns a custom HTTP response](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-fixed-response-action) and drops the request, so users still have to retype the address.
- "Create a second Application Load Balancer with an ...": One load balancer can listen on [HTTP port 80](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb) and [HTTPS port 443](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-faq-http-and-https-one-alb), and users would not type a second name anyway.

**Twin.** If the stem said "users of the HTTPS site must be sent to an old HTTP site" instead: no redirect action fits, because [You cannot redirect HTTPS to HTTP](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https).

**Takeaway.** An HTTP listener with a redirect action moves users to HTTPS without code changes.

**Review.** [Listener rules are checked in priority order and the default rule comes last](2-deep.md#listener-rules-are-checked-in-priority-order-and-the-default-rule-comes-last-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q022 -->
### Question 11

A company has several VPCs in one AWS Region and a central security VPC. Security policy requires that all traffic into and out of each VPC passes through a fleet of third-party firewall appliances that run on Amazon EC2 instances. The fleet must be scalable as traffic grows, and the company wants to centrally manage the appliances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create a Gateway Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, add Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in each VPC, and route traffic to the endpoints.
- Create a Network Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, and point every client and application at the DNS name of that load balancer.
- Create an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL in each VPC, and send all inbound web requests through that load balancer.
- Create a separate Gateway Load Balancer and a separate fleet of appliances in each VPC, and route the traffic of each VPC through its own fleet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a Gateway Load Balancer for the appliances in the security VPC, add Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in each VPC, and route traffic to the endpoints.

**Deciding phrases.** "third-party firewall appliances", "all traffic into and out of each VPC", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The traffic is not addressed to the appliances, so this is a Gateway Load Balancer case: it is for [deploying inline virtual appliances](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) and [transparently passes all Layer 3 traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances) through them. Endpoints in each VPC receive the traffic from route tables, and the appliances stay [centralized in one location](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-endpoint-centralize-appliances).

**Why not.**

- "Create a Network Load Balancer for the appliances ...": Traffic between other hosts is not sent to the load balancer's name, so it bypasses the appliances; inline appliances need a load balancer that is [invisible to the source and destination](../facts/elb.md#elb-gwlb-faq-when-inline-appliances).
- "Create an Application Load Balancer with an AWS ...": AWS WAF can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb) to the load balancer, but the policy requires third-party appliances for all traffic of each VPC.
- "Create a separate Gateway Load Balancer and a ...": It works, but a load balancer and a fleet in every VPC multiply the appliances to patch and scale, where endpoints share one central fleet.

**Twin.** If the stem said "filter the HTTP requests to the company's web application" instead: an Application Load Balancer with an AWS WAF web ACL, because it can [block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-waf-integrates-with-alb).

**Takeaway.** All traffic through third-party appliances, steered by route tables: a Gateway Load Balancer with endpoints in each VPC.

**Review.** [A Gateway Load Balancer passes packets through appliances without changing them](2-deep.md#a-gateway-load-balancer-passes-packets-through-appliances-without-changing-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q014 -->
### Question 12

A company runs a three-tier application in one VPC. The internet-facing web tier runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and users must reach it through one endpoint. The web tier calls the application tier, which also runs on EC2 instances. Each tier must scale on its own. The application tier must be reachable privately from the web tier and must stay unreachable from the internet. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Add a listener rule to the internet-facing load balancer that forwards /app/* requests to a target group of the application tier instances.
- Give the application tier instances public IP addresses in public subnets so that the internet-facing load balancer can reach them as targets.
- Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets, and register the web tier instances in its target group.
- Launch Amazon EC2 instances that run open source proxy software in private subnets, and have them spread the web tier's calls over the application tier.
- Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, register the application tier instances, and point the web tier's calls at it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in public subnets, and register the web tier instances in its target group.
- Create an internal Application Load Balancer in private subnets, register the application tier instances, and point the web tier's calls at it.

**Deciding phrases.** "must be reachable privately from the web tier", "Each tier must scale on its own", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS describes this pattern for multi-tier applications, with [both internal and internet-facing load balancers](../facts/elb.md#elb-multi-tier-internet-facing-plus-internal). The web instances register with the internet-facing load balancer and send their calls to the internal one, which forwards them to the application tier. Each tier scales behind its own load balancer, and the application tier has no public entry point.

- Its nodes [have public IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internet-facing-nodes-public-ips) and accept users from the internet, and the web instances behind it can stay in private subnets.
- Internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only), so only [clients with access to the VPC](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only) reach the application tier.

**Why not.**

- "Add a listener rule to the internet-facing load ...": A path rule on the internet-facing load balancer lets any user on the internet reach the application tier with a /app/* request.
- "Give the application tier instances public IP addresses ...": Targets are reached [using private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-targets-need-no-public-ip), so public addresses only add exposure for the application tier.
- "Launch Amazon EC2 instances that run open source ...": It works, but the company has to run, patch and scale the proxy instances itself, which an internal load balancer avoids.

**Twin.** If the stem said "partners on the internet also call the application tier" instead: the application tier needs an internet-facing load balancer too, because internal nodes [have only private IP addresses](../facts/elb.md#elb-internal-nodes-private-ips-only).

**Takeaway.** A private tier behind a public tier: an internet-facing load balancer for the web tier and an internal one for the application tier.

**Review.** [Targets can stay private and accept traffic only from the load balancer](2-deep.md#targets-can-stay-private-and-accept-traffic-only-from-the-load-balancer-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q016 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a TCP service on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer that was created with default settings. The instances run across multiple Availability Zones: 2 instances in Availability Zone A and 6 instances in Availability Zone B. Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes. The 2 instances in Availability Zone A are overloaded, and the other instances are mostly idle. The company must spread connections evenly over all 8 instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add 2 instances in each Availability Zone, because cross-zone load balancing is already turned on for every type of load balancer.
- Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group, and accept the charge for data that crosses between Availability Zones.
- Change the routing algorithm of the target group to least outstanding requests so that new connections go to the least busy instances.
- Launch 4 more instances in Availability Zone A, and keep the same number of instances in each zone whenever the fleet changes size.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on cross-zone load balancing for the target group, and accept the charge for data that crosses between Availability Zones.

**Deciding phrases.** "created with default settings", "Client connections are spread evenly over the two load balancer nodes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** With cross-zone load balancing off, each node uses the [registered targets in its Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-cross-zone-what-it-does). The two nodes get the same number of connections, so each of the 2 instances in Availability Zone A carries three times the load of an instance in Availability Zone B. On a Network Load Balancer you can turn cross-zone load balancing [on or off at the target group level](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-cross-zone-lb-and-tg-level).

**Why not.**

- "Add 2 instances in each Availability Zone, because ...": On a Network Load Balancer, [cross-zone load balancing is disabled by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-gwlb-cross-zone-off-by-default), so each node still uses the instances of its own zone, and the load stays uneven.
- "Change the routing algorithm of the target group ...": A Network Load Balancer selects a target [using a flow hash algorithm](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-flow-hash-target-selection); [least outstanding requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-routing-algorithms-three) is an algorithm of Application Load Balancer target groups.
- "Launch 4 more instances in Availability Zone A, ...": It works, but the team has to keep both zones equal at every change, where one setting spreads connections over all instances.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an Application Load Balancer" instead: no change is needed, because cross-zone load balancing is [on by default](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-cross-zone-on-by-default) for it.

**Takeaway.** Uneven instance counts per zone behind an NLB: turn on cross-zone load balancing and pay for the data between zones.

**Review.** [Cross-zone load balancing spreads requests over the targets in every enabled zone](2-deep.md#cross-zone-load-balancing-spreads-requests-over-the-targets-in-every-enabled-zone-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q020 -->
### Question 14

A company's website runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The HTTPS listener uses a certificate that a third-party certificate authority issued and that the company imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Last year the certificate expired, and the website was unavailable until an engineer imported a new certificate. The company wants to automate certificate renewal so that this outage does not happen again. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the imported certificate on the listener, and rely on ACM managed renewal to renew the certificate before it expires.
- Upload the third-party certificate to IAM, and change the HTTPS listener to use the IAM certificate instead of the ACM certificate.
- Request a public certificate for the domain from ACM, and replace the imported certificate on the HTTPS listener with it.
- Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that buys a new certificate from the third-party authority every year and imports it into ACM.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Request a public certificate for the domain from ACM, and replace the imported certificate on the HTTPS listener with it.

**Deciding phrases.** "imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)", "automate certificate renewal", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The outage came from a manual step. For an imported certificate, ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal), and [you must monitor the expiration date](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically). A certificate that ACM issues and deploys on the load balancer [can be renewed automatically](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-acm-certs-renew-automatically), and new requests then use the renewed certificate.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the imported certificate on the listener, and ...": ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates, so the company still has to renew this one itself.
- "Upload the third-party certificate to IAM, and change ...": You can [upload the certificate](../facts/acm.md#acm-alb-certificate-from-acm-or-iam) to IAM, but that changes where it is stored, not who renews it; the company still renews it.
- "Create a scheduled AWS Lambda function that buys ...": It works, but the company has to write and fix code that buys and imports certificates, where an ACM certificate renews itself.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company must keep its current certificate authority" instead: a scheduled re-import becomes the answer, because ACM [does not manage the renewal process](../facts/acm.md#acm-faq-imported-no-managed-renewal) for imported certificates.

**Takeaway.** ACM renews the certificates it issues, not the ones you import; use an ACM certificate to automate renewal.

**Review.** [An HTTPS listener decrypts requests at the load balancer with its certificate](2-deep.md#an-https-listener-decrypts-requests-at-the-load-balancer-with-its-certificate-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q013 -->
### Question 15

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps each user's session data in the memory of the instance that served the user's first request. Users are signed out when a later request reaches a different instance. The company wants a fix as soon as possible, with minimal code changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, so that the load balancer sends all requests of a user to the same instance.
- Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster that every instance reads and writes, and change the application to use the cluster.
- Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, and turn on source IP stickiness for the target group of the instances.
- Run a session database on one new EC2 instance that every web instance reads and writes, and change the application to use that database.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, so that the load balancer sends all requests of a user to the same instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "session data in the memory of the instance", "as soon as possible, with minimal code changes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), so each user returns to the instance that holds the session in memory. The target group offers [duration-based cookies and application-based cookies](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-duration-vs-application-cookie); both kinds send a user back to one target, and the duration-based kind needs no cookie from the application. It is one setting on the target group, so the fix is live quickly and needs no code.

**Why not.**

- "Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache ...": It works and is the better long-term design, but it needs code changes and a new cluster, so it is not the fastest fix.
- "Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network ...": It replaces the load balancer, and source IP stickiness can cause [uneven distribution of connections and flows](../facts/elb.md#elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat) when many users share one NAT address.
- "Run a session database on one new EC2 ...": It needs code changes, and the team patches and scales the database instance itself, which is more work than one target group setting.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Users must keep their sessions when an instance is terminated, so the web tier must become stateless and scalable" instead: ElastiCache, because AWS calls a [centralized session management data store](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers) the ideal answer.

**Takeaway.** For a fast fix without code changes, turn on stickiness for the target group.

**Review.** [Sticky sessions send a user back to one target and bypass the algorithm](2-deep.md#sticky-sessions-send-a-user-back-to-one-target-and-bypass-the-algorithm-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q021 -->
### Question 16

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. The instances have public IP addresses and are registered as instance targets of an internet-facing Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443. The load balancer was created years ago without security groups. The instances' security group allows TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. The company must restrict access so that the instances accept traffic on port 443 from a load balancer and from no other source. Clients must keep reaching the application through a load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?

- Associate a new security group with the existing Network Load Balancer, and allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group.
- Keep the rule that allows port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, because a Network Load Balancer has no security group that a target rule can reference.
- Move the instances to private subnets without public IP addresses, and keep the rule that allows port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the instances.
- Create a new Network Load Balancer with a security group, allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a new Network Load Balancer with a security group, allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to it.

**Deciding phrases.** "created years ago without security groups", "allows TCP port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0", "from a load balancer and from no other source", "MOST secure"

**Why.** A Network Load Balancer gets security groups [when you create it](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation); for one created without them, [you can't associate them](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) later. A new load balancer with a security group lets the instance rule name [the load balancer's security group as the source](../facts/elb.md#elb-target-sg-reference-lb-sg). Clients then reach the instances [through your Network Load Balancer](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access), and the rule [prevents them from sending traffic directly](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-sg-reference-blocks-direct-access).

**Why not.**

- "Associate a new security group with the existing ...": The load balancer was created without security groups, and for such a load balancer [you can't associate them](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) later.
- "Keep the rule that allows port 443 from ...": A Network Load Balancer can get security groups [when you create it](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation), so targets can reference one; this option restricts nothing.
- "Move the instances to private subnets without public ...": Private subnets remove the internet path, but any resource in the VPC can still reach port 443 on the instances, so they accept traffic from more than a load balancer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the load balancer was created with a security group" instead: keep it and reference its security group in the instance rule, because you can [change the security groups](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation) of such a load balancer.

**Takeaway.** A Network Load Balancer gets security groups at creation; to add them later, create a new load balancer.

**Review.** [Targets can stay private and accept traffic only from the load balancer](2-deep.md#targets-can-stay-private-and-accept-traffic-only-from-the-load-balancer-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q019 -->
### Question 17

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Cross-zone load balancing is turned off for the target group, and zonal shift is turned on for the load balancer. During an incident, responses from the instances in one Availability Zone become slow, but those instances still pass their health checks. The company must move traffic away from that Availability Zone as soon as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Start a zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) for the load balancer, away from the Availability Zone with the slow instances.
- Wait for the target group health checks to mark the slow instances as unhealthy, so that the load balancer stops routing requests to them.
- Deregister the instances in that Availability Zone from the target group one at a time, and register them again after the incident ends.
- Create a new Application Load Balancer in the two healthy Availability Zones, register their instances, and point the DNS record of the website at it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Start a zonal shift in Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) for the load balancer, away from the Availability Zone with the slow instances.

**Deciding phrases.** "still pass their health checks", "move traffic away from that Availability Zone", "as soon as possible", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Zonal shift, a capability of [Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what), moves traffic [away from an impaired Availability Zone](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what) [with a single action](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-shift-what). For a load balancer with cross-zone load balancing turned off, AWS Well-Architected names ARC [to provide zonal shift capability](../facts/elb.md#elb-wa-rel10-cross-zone-off-use-zonal-shift). The two other zones keep serving. Health checks do not help, because the slow instances still pass them.

**Why not.**

- "Wait for the target group health checks to ...": The instances pass their checks, and the load balancer [routes traffic only to the healthy targets](../facts/elb.md#elb-routes-only-to-healthy-targets), so it keeps sending them requests.
- "Deregister the instances in that Availability Zone from ...": It works, but every target is a manual step, and by default the load balancer [waits 300 seconds](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-deregistration-waits-for-in-flight) before it completes each deregistration.
- "Create a new Application Load Balancer in the ...": It works in the end, but a new load balancer, its listeners and a DNS change take longer than one action on the current load balancer.

**Twin.** If the stem said "AWS should move the traffic when its own monitoring finds an impaired zone" instead: zonal autoshift, because then [you authorize AWS to shift away resource traffic](../facts/elb.md#elb-zonal-autoshift-aws-shifts).

**Takeaway.** To drain one impaired Availability Zone fast, start a zonal shift on the load balancer.

**Review.** [Cross-zone load balancing spreads requests over the targets in every enabled zone](2-deep.md#cross-zone-load-balancing-spreads-requests-over-the-targets-in-every-enabled-zone-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=elb-q017 -->
### Question 18

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. The application keeps each user's session data in the memory of the instance that served the user's first request. Users are signed out when a later request reaches a different instance. Users must keep their sessions when an instance is terminated, so the web tier must become stateless and scalable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, so that the load balancer sends all requests of a user to the same instance.
- Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster that every instance reads and writes, and change the application to use the cluster.
- Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer, and turn on source IP stickiness for the target group of the instances.
- Run a session database on one new EC2 instance that every web instance reads and writes, and change the application to use that database.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Store the session data in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster that every instance reads and writes, and change the application to use the cluster.

**Deciding phrases.** "session data in the memory of the instance", "keep their sessions when an instance is terminated", "stateless and scalable", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** To make a web tier stateless, AWS says to offload session data to a [database, cache, or external files](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data). AWS calls a [centralized session management data store](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers) the ideal solution [when your fleet of web servers is elastic](../facts/elb.md#elb-session-store-centralized-not-on-servers). A managed ElastiCache cluster keeps the sessions when Auto Scaling terminates an instance, and the team runs no database instance of its own.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on duration-based stickiness for the target group, ...": Sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), so the session is lost with that instance at scale-in.
- "Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network ...": Source IP stickiness still keeps the session on one instance, and it can cause [uneven distribution of connections and flows](../facts/elb.md#elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat).
- "Run a session database on one new EC2 ...": It works, but the team patches and scales one self-managed database instance, and that instance becomes a single point of failure for every session.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The company wants a fix as soon as possible, with minimal code changes" instead: duration-based stickiness, because sticky sessions [bind a user's session to a specific target](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what) without code changes.

**Takeaway.** To keep sessions through scale-in, move them to a shared store such as ElastiCache; stickiness does not keep them.

**Review.** [Sticky sessions send a user back to one target and bypass the algorithm](2-deep.md#sticky-sessions-send-a-user-back-to-one-target-and-bypass-the-algorithm-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
